h1.content:
Convened by the Emperor Constantine, the First Council of Nicaea was the first ecumenical council of the Christian Church. It was called primarily to address the Arian controversy, which questioned the divinity of Christ, and produced the original Nicene Creed affirming that the Son is "of one substance" with the Father.

The council also addressed questions of Church discipline and the dating of Easter, setting a precedent for resolving doctrinal disputes through gathered councils of bishops.

h2.content:
St. Benedict of Nursia founded the monastery of Monte Cassino and wrote a Rule for monastic life balancing prayer, manual labor, and communal living under the motto ora et labora, "pray and work." The Rule’s moderation and practicality made it the dominant model for Western monasticism for centuries.

Benedictine monasteries became centers of learning, agriculture, and the preservation of classical and religious texts throughout the early medieval period, earning Benedict the title of patron of Europe.

h3.content:
Long-building tensions between the Latin-speaking Church centered in Rome and the Greek-speaking Church centered in Constantinople came to a head in 1054, when mutual excommunications were exchanged between Pope Leo IX’s legate and Patriarch Michael Cerularius. Disputes over papal authority, the filioque clause in the Creed, and liturgical practice underlay the break.

The schism formally divided Western (Roman Catholic) and Eastern (Orthodox) Christianity, a division that persists today despite ongoing dialogue toward reconciliation.

h4.content:
Called in response to the Protestant Reformation, the Council of Trent met intermittently over eighteen years to clarify Catholic doctrine and reform Church discipline. It reaffirmed the seven sacraments, the authority of Scripture and Tradition together, and addressed abuses such as the sale of indulgences.

Trent shaped Catholic identity and practice for the next four centuries, standardizing the liturgy in what became known as the Tridentine Mass.

h5.content:
Convened by Pope John XXIII and concluded under Pope Paul VI, the Second Vatican Council was called to renew the Church’s engagement with the modern world. It produced sixteen documents addressing the liturgy, the nature of the Church, religious freedom, and relations with other faiths.

Among its most visible effects was the reform of the liturgy, including the introduction of Mass celebrated in vernacular languages alongside Latin.

h6.content:
Fifty days after the Resurrection, the Holy Spirit descended on the apostles gathered with Mary in Jerusalem. According to Acts 2, Peter preached to crowds of pilgrims from across the Roman world, each of whom heard in his own language, and about three thousand were baptized.

Pentecost is often called the birthday of the Church. The first community devoted itself to "the apostles’ teaching and fellowship, to the breaking of bread and the prayers."

h7.content:
As Gentiles began entering the Church, a dispute arose over whether they needed to be circumcised and keep the full Mosaic Law. Paul and Barnabas went to Jerusalem, where the apostles and elders met with Peter and James.

The council decided that Gentile converts need not be circumcised, asking only that they avoid a few practices. It is the model for all later councils and opened the way for the Church’s mission to the whole world.

h8.content:
Over roughly a decade, Paul traveled thousands of miles through Asia Minor, Macedonia, and Greece, founding communities in cities like Philippi, Thessalonica, Corinth, and Ephesus.

His letters to these churches, written between about 50 and 65, are the earliest Christian writings we have. He was eventually arrested in Jerusalem, appealed to Caesar, and was taken to Rome.

h9.content:
After a great fire devastated Rome in 64, the Emperor Nero blamed the Christians, launching the first imperial persecution. The historian Tacitus records Christians being torn apart by dogs, crucified, and burned as torches.

According to ancient tradition, Peter was crucified upside down on the Vatican Hill, and Paul, a Roman citizen, was beheaded on the road to Ostia. St. Peter’s Basilica stands over Peter’s tomb.

h10.content:
During the Jewish revolt against Rome, the legions of Titus besieged Jerusalem and destroyed the Second Temple in the year 70, fulfilling Jesus’ prophecy that not one stone would be left upon another.

The event hastened the separation of Christianity from Judaism and shifted the center of the Christian world away from Jerusalem toward cities like Antioch, Alexandria, and Rome.

h11.content:
The 27 books of the New Testament were written between about 50 and 100. Paul’s letters came first, followed by the Gospels of Mark, Matthew, and Luke, and finally the Gospel of John and the Book of Revelation.

The Church gradually recognized which writings were apostolic and inspired. The list of 27 books is found in St. Athanasius’s Easter letter of 367 and was affirmed by regional councils at Rome, Hippo, and Carthage at the end of the fourth century.

h12.content:
For two and a half centuries, Christianity was an illegal religion in the Roman Empire. Persecution was sporadic and local at first, but became empire-wide under Decius (250) and Valerian (257–258), and reached its peak in the Great Persecution under Diocletian beginning in 303.

Christians buried their dead in the catacombs outside Rome and honored their martyrs’ tombs. Tertullian wrote that "the blood of martyrs is the seed of Christians," and the Church continued to grow.

h13.content:
Around 270, St. Anthony of Egypt gave away his possessions and withdrew into the desert. Thousands followed, living as hermits or in communities organized by St. Pachomius.

The sayings of these Desert Fathers and Mothers became spiritual classics, and pilgrims such as John Cassian carried the monastic ideal to the West.

h14.content:
After his victory at the Milvian Bridge in 312, which he attributed to the God of the Christians, Emperor Constantine agreed with his co-emperor Licinius to grant religious toleration throughout the empire.

Christians could now worship openly and recover confiscated property. Constantine built great churches, including the first St. Peter’s in Rome and the Church of the Holy Sepulchre in Jerusalem.

h15.content:
The second ecumenical council, called by Emperor Theodosius I, reaffirmed the faith of Nicaea after decades of Arian controversy. Drawing on the theology of the Cappadocian Fathers, it proclaimed the full divinity of the Holy Spirit.

Its expanded creed, the Niceno-Constantinopolitan Creed, is the Nicene Creed recited at Mass every Sunday.

h16.content:
Commissioned by Pope Damasus I, St. Jerome began revising the Latin Gospels in 382, then spent years in Bethlehem translating the Old Testament directly from the Hebrew.

His Vulgate became the standard Bible of the Western Church for over a thousand years, and the Council of Trent declared it the authentic Latin text.

h17.content:
The Council of Ephesus (431) rejected the teaching of Nestorius and affirmed that Mary is Theotokos, "God-bearer," because the child she bore is truly God.

The Council of Chalcedon (451), guided by Pope Leo the Great’s Tome, defined that Christ is one person in two natures, fully divine and fully human, "without confusion, change, division, or separation." Some Eastern Churches did not accept Chalcedon, producing a lasting division.

h18.content:
Germanic peoples settled across the Western Empire during the fifth century. Rome was sacked by the Visigoths in 410, prompting Augustine to write The City of God, and again by the Vandals in 455. In 476 the last Western emperor was deposed.

As Roman administration collapsed, bishops and monasteries often became the guardians of order, learning, and care for the poor.

h19.content:
Clovis, king of the Franks, was baptized by St. Remigius at Reims, likely around 496, encouraged by his Christian wife St. Clotilde. Unlike most Germanic rulers, who were Arian Christians, Clovis embraced Catholic Christianity.

His conversion made the Franks allies of the papacy and earned France the title "eldest daughter of the Church."

h20.content:
Elected pope in 590 during plague and invasion, Gregory reorganized the Church’s charity and administration. In 597 he sent St. Augustine of Canterbury and a band of monks to the Anglo-Saxons.

King Ethelbert of Kent was baptized, and Canterbury became the seat of the English Church. Irish monks from Iona and Lindisfarne evangelized the north at the same time.

h21.content:
Within a century of Muhammad’s death in 632, Arab armies conquered the Holy Land, Syria, Egypt, North Africa, and most of Spain, lands that had been among the oldest centers of Christianity.

The ancient patriarchates of Alexandria, Antioch, and Jerusalem came under Muslim rule. Christian communities survived but gradually became minorities. The advance into Western Europe was halted at the Battle of Tours in 732.

h22.content:
In 726 Byzantine Emperor Leo III began a campaign against religious images, which some viewed as idolatry. Icons were destroyed and their defenders persecuted.

The Second Council of Nicaea (787), the seventh ecumenical council, taught that icons may be venerated, since the honor given to an image passes to the one it represents. The final restoration of icons in 843 is still celebrated in the East as the Triumph of Orthodoxy.

h23.content:
On Christmas Day 800, Pope Leo III crowned Charlemagne, king of the Franks, as emperor in St. Peter’s Basilica. The act created a Western empire allied with the papacy.

Charlemagne promoted the Carolingian Renaissance, founding schools and preserving classical and Christian texts.

h24.content:
Duke William of Aquitaine founded the Benedictine abbey of Cluny in Burgundy in 910, placing it directly under the pope’s protection and outside the control of local lords and bishops.

Cluny became the center of a vast network of monasteries known for elaborate liturgy and reform, and it produced several popes.

h25.content:
Prince Vladimir of Kyiv was baptized in 988 and ordered the mass baptism of his people in the Dnieper River. According to the chronicle, his envoys to Constantinople’s Hagia Sophia reported that "we knew not whether we were in heaven or on earth."

This event is the origin of Christianity among the Ukrainian, Belarusian, and Russian peoples.

h26.content:
Pope Gregory VII worked to free the Church from lay control, combat the buying and selling of Church offices, and enforce clerical celibacy. His claim that only the Church could appoint bishops led to a clash with Emperor Henry IV.

Henry, excommunicated, famously stood barefoot in the snow at Canossa in 1077 seeking absolution. The dispute was largely settled by the Concordat of Worms in 1122.

h27.content:
In 1095 Pope Urban II called on Western knights to aid the Byzantine Empire and to recover Jerusalem. The First Crusade captured the city in 1099, with terrible massacres. Later crusades failed to hold the Holy Land, and the last crusader stronghold fell in 1291.

The Fourth Crusade’s sack of Christian Constantinople in 1204 deepened the rift between East and West. In 2000, Pope John Paul II asked forgiveness for sins committed by Christians, including during the Crusades.

h28.content:
Cathedral schools grew into the first universities at Bologna, Paris, and Oxford. Scholars such as Anselm, Peter Lombard, Albert the Great, Thomas Aquinas, and Bonaventure used logic and the rediscovered works of Aristotle to explore the faith systematically.

The Gothic cathedrals of the same period, such as Chartres and Notre-Dame de Paris, expressed the same confidence in an ordered world pointing to God.

h29.content:
St. Francis of Assisi’s brotherhood was approved in 1209, and St. Dominic’s Order of Preachers in 1216. Unlike monks bound to one monastery, these friars lived in poverty, begged for their food, and preached in the growing towns.

The Carmelites and Augustinian friars soon followed. The friars renewed popular preaching, staffed universities, and led missions across the known world.

h30.content:
Called by Pope Innocent III, the Fourth Lateran Council was the largest council of the Middle Ages. It defined the Real Presence using the word "transubstantiation."

It also required Catholics to confess and receive Communion at least once a year, the origin of the "Easter duty," and it ordered reforms of clergy and preaching.

h31.content:
Amid violence in Italy and pressure from the French crown, Pope Clement V settled in Avignon in 1309. Seven popes, all French, reigned from there for nearly seventy years.

Critics called it the "Babylonian Captivity" of the Church. St. Catherine of Siena and St. Bridget of Sweden urged the popes to return, and Gregory XI finally returned to Rome in 1377.

h32.content:
After Gregory XI’s death, a disputed election produced two rival popes, one in Rome and one in Avignon. An attempt to resolve the crisis at Pisa in 1409 resulted in a third claimant.

The Council of Constance (1414–1418) ended the schism by securing the resignation or deposition of the claimants and electing Martin V in 1417.

h33.content:
With the Byzantine Empire threatened by the Ottoman Turks, Greek and Latin bishops met at Ferrara and Florence and in 1439 signed a decree of reunion. Agreements with Armenian, Coptic, and other Eastern Churches followed.

The union was widely rejected in the East and collapsed after Constantinople fell to the Ottomans in 1453, but it served as a model for later Eastern Catholic Churches.

h34.content:
Following Columbus’s voyage in 1492, Spanish and Portuguese missionaries brought the faith to the Americas. Friars such as Bartolomé de las Casas denounced the brutal treatment of Indigenous peoples, and in 1537 Pope Paul III declared that they must not be deprived of their liberty or property.

The apparition of Our Lady of Guadalupe to St. Juan Diego in 1531 was followed by the conversion of millions in Mexico. Today most of the world’s Catholics live in the Americas, Africa, and Asia.

h35.content:
On October 31, 1517, Martin Luther, an Augustinian friar, circulated his 95 Theses criticizing the sale of indulgences. The dispute grew into a break with Rome over authority, justification, and the sacraments.

Within decades, Lutheran, Reformed (Calvinist), and Anabaptist churches had formed across northern Europe. The division of Western Christianity shaped European politics and wars for over a century.

h36.content:
When Pope Clement VII would not annul Henry VIII’s marriage to Catherine of Aragon, Parliament passed the Act of Supremacy in 1534, making the king head of the Church in England. Thomas More and John Fisher were executed for refusing to accept it.

Monasteries were dissolved, and after a Catholic restoration under Mary I, Elizabeth I established the Church of England. English Catholics faced fines, imprisonment, and death for over two centuries.

h37.content:
Pope Paul III approved St. Ignatius of Loyola’s Society of Jesus in 1540. The Jesuits founded schools and universities across Europe and sent missionaries such as St. Francis Xavier to India and Japan and Matteo Ricci to China.

With reformers like Teresa of Ávila, Charles Borromeo, Philip Neri, and Francis de Sales, they led a great renewal of Catholic life known as the Catholic (or Counter-) Reformation.

h38.content:
On October 7, 1571, the fleet of the Holy League, organized by Pope Pius V, defeated the Ottoman navy off the coast of Greece, halting Ottoman naval expansion in the Mediterranean.

Pius V had asked all of Christendom to pray the Rosary for victory, and he established a feast in thanksgiving. It is celebrated today as Our Lady of the Rosary on October 7.

h39.content:
The Revolution confiscated Church property, dissolved religious orders, and in 1790 required priests to swear an oath to the state. Thousands of priests, religious, and laypeople who refused were exiled or killed, including the Carmelite nuns of Compiègne, guillotined in 1794.

Napoleon’s Concordat of 1801 restored the Church in France, but the Revolution began a long struggle between the Church and secular governments across Europe.

h40.content:
On December 8, 1854, Pope Pius IX solemnly defined that the Virgin Mary was preserved free from original sin from the first moment of her conception.

Four years later, at Lourdes, Mary appeared to St. Bernadette Soubirous and said, "I am the Immaculate Conception." Lourdes became one of the world’s greatest pilgrimage sites.
